pos: n. (chief town of the Waldensian valleys in Piedmont; seat of the Waldensian synod)
etymology: From Italian torre, a tower, and the river Pellice; the valley name in Piedmontese Val Pelis.
biblical_def: Torre Pellice is the principal town of the Val Pellice and the administrative centre of the Waldensian church. The Waldenses had held the three valleys of Pellice, Chisone and Germanasca since the thirteenth century, dissenting from Rome before the Reformation existed, and they survived there through crusade, inquisition, massacre and exile until the Letters Patent of 1848 gave them civil rights; the synod and the Table, their governing body, have met in Torre Pellice since, with a college, a library and a hospital in the town. The dictionary records it because the Waldensian valleys are the plainest European instance of a doctrine Scripture states repeatedly and the church forgets in every prosperous generation: that God preserves a remnant, and that the remnant is small, and that its survival is not its own achievement. “Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a remnant as that which is left, a residue; election as the choice of God in selecting a person or persons to his favour; and a valley as a hollow or low tract of land between hills.
webster_full: REMNANT, n. [from remain.] That which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part; residue.
ELECTION, n. [L. electio.] The choice of God, by which persons are distinguished as objects of mercy; divine choice.
VALLEY, n. [L. vallis.] A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.
SYNOD, n. [Gr. an assembly.] A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
scriptures: Rom 11:5
Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
Isa 1:9
Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah.
Rom 9:27
Esaias also crieth concerning Israel, Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved:
Rev 12:6
And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she hath a place prepared of God, that they should feed her there a thousand two hundred and threescore days.
corruption_summary: The Waldensian capital in the Val Pellice; the synod and Table have met here since the civil rights of 1848.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is Rome's treatment of the Waldenses as heretics to be exterminated, which was pursued by crusade in 1487, by the Inquisition for three centuries, and by massacre as late as 1655 and 1686. The dictionary names it plainly and does not accept the modern framing in which this becomes a regrettable misunderstanding on both sides. A second and gentler corruption threatens the valleys now: a church that survived by doctrine being commended chiefly for its tolerance and its tourism.

The principle to recover is that the preservation of a remnant is God's work and the measure of His mercy, not of the remnant's strength. Isaiah makes the remnant the only reason Judah was not Sodom: “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom” (Isa 1:9). Paul quotes him to the same end, that of a multitude “a remnant shall be saved” (Rom 9:27). And John sees the church kept alive in a prepared place, where “the woman fled into the wilderness, where she hath a place prepared of God” (Rev 12:6). Elijah was told that seven thousand were left, “all the knees which have not bowed unto Baal” (1Ki 19:18), and he had not known of one.

pos: n. (Waldensian valley in Piedmont; where the synod of Chanforan in 1532 joined the Waldenses to the Reformation)
etymology: From Piedmontese Angrogna, the name of the valley and its torrent.
biblical_def: Angrogna is the valley in which the Waldenses stopped being a secret society and became a Reformed church. At the meadow of Chanforan in September 1532, their barbes, the itinerant preachers who had carried the old dissent from house to house for three centuries, met with Guillaume Farel and Antoine Saunier from Switzerland and resolved to adopt the Reformed confession, to abandon the practices of concealment, to hold public worship, and to pay for a new translation of the whole Bible into French. The money they voted, a very large sum for a mountain people, produced Olivetan's French Bible of 1535, from which the whole French Protestant tradition descends. The dictionary records Angrogna because the decision to stop hiding is a decision Christ requires, and because the first act of the newly public church was to fund the Scriptures. “What I tell you in darkness, that speak ye in light” (Mat 10:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a barbe as an uncle, used by the Waldenses as the title of their pastors; manifest as plain, open, clearly visible; and bold as daring, courageous, confident.
webster_full: MANIFEST, adj. [L. manifestus.] Plain; open; clearly visible to the eye or obvious to the understanding; apparent; not obscure.
HOUSETOP, n. The top or roof of a house; in the East, a flat roof used as a place of resort.
BOLD, adj. Daring; courageous; brave; intrepid; fearless; requiring courage in the execution.
BUSHEL, n. A dry measure containing eight gallons or four pecks; also, the vessel of that capacity.
scriptures: What I tell you in darkness, that speak ye in light: and what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops.
Luk 8:17
For nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest; neither any thing hid, that shall not be known and come abroad.
Mat 5:15
Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.
Pro 28:1
The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
corruption_summary: Where the Waldensian synod of 1532 adopted the Reformed confession, ended its concealment, and paid for Olivetan's French Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption that Chanforan renounced was the one three centuries of persecution had made necessary and then habitual: a faith held in private, confessed outwardly in the forms of a church one did not believe, with the real teaching passed from barbe to household in the dark. The Waldenses had good reasons, and the dictionary does not judge the fathers who hid. But the practice had begun to corrupt the doctrine, and the men of 1532 knew it, which is why they ended it at the same meeting at which they bought a Bible.

The principle to recover is that the gospel is given to be published and will be published whatever men prefer. Christ states the law of disclosure as a fact about the universe: “For nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest” (Luk 8:17). He uses the ordinary sense of a householder to make the point, since “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick” (Mat 5:15). And Proverbs contrasts the two kinds of nerve: “The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion” (Pro 28:1).

“The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion” (Pro 28:1) — the money voted that paid for Olivetan's Bible of 1535.

pos: n. (uppermost village of the Val Pellice, Piedmont; the last Waldensian settlement before the French passes)
etymology: From Italian Bobbio, a settlement name of uncertain origin, with the river Pellice.
biblical_def: Bobbio Pellice stands at the head of the Val Pellice where the valley narrows to the passes into France, and that position made it the Waldenses' last refuge in every persecution. When the troops came up the valley the people of the lower villages withdrew through Bobbio into the high pastures and the caves above it, and from there over into the Queyras; the Glorious Return of 1689 came back the same way, Henri Arnaud leading some nine hundred men over the passes to retake the valleys they had been expelled from three years before. The dictionary records the village because the mountain refuge is a literal fact of Waldensian history and a figure the New Testament uses without embarrassment. Of the persecuted faithful Hebrews says what no modern tribute would dare: “they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth” (Heb 11:38), and adds that the world was not worthy of them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a refuge as shelter or protection from danger; a den as a cave or hollow place in the earth; and a wilderness as a desert, a tract of land uncultivated and uninhabited.
webster_full: REFUGE, n. [L. refugium.] Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger.
DEN, n. A cave or hollow place in the earth; usually applied to the cave or habitation of a wild beast.
WILDERNESS, n. A desert; a tract of land or region uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings.
PASS, n. A narrow passage, entrance or avenue; a narrow or difficult place of entrance and exit.
scriptures: (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Get thee hence, and turn thee eastward, and hide thyself by the brook Cherith, that is before Jordan.
Psa 9:9
The LORD also will be a refuge for the oppressed, a refuge in times of trouble.
And there is hope in thine end, saith the LORD, that thy children shall come again to their own border.
corruption_summary: The highest Waldensian village, refuge in every persecution and the road of the Glorious Return of 1689.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The nearer error is the romance of the mountain church, which turns three centuries of hunger, exposure and child mortality into scenery. The caves above Bobbio were not picturesque to the families in them. The Waldenses did not seek the heights; they were driven there, and the valley people have always told the story as a judgment to be survived rather than an adventure to be admired.

The principle to recover is that God appoints hiding places and brings His people home from them. Elijah was sent into concealment by direct command: “Get thee hence, and turn thee eastward, and hide thyself by the brook Cherith” (1Ki 17:3). The psalmist names the refuge that is not geographical, for “The LORD also will be a refuge for the oppressed, a refuge in times of trouble” (Psa 9:9). And Jeremiah gives the exiles the promise the Return of 1689 took literally: “there is hope in thine end, saith the LORD, that thy children shall come again to their own border” (Jer 31:17).

“The LORD also will be a refuge for the oppressed, a refuge in times of trouble” (Psa 9:9) — the passes into the Queyras.

pos: n. (fortress town of Piedmont at the mouth of the Waldensian valleys; seat of the tribunals and garrisons that persecuted them)
etymology: From Italian Pinerolo, from pino, a pine; the little pine wood.
biblical_def: Pinerolo sits where the Waldensian valleys open onto the Piedmontese plain, and for four centuries it was the place the troops came from. The Savoyard dukes garrisoned it, the French held it from 1631 to 1696 and built the citadel in which prisoners of state were kept, and the Inquisition's commissions against the valleys were issued and its sentences executed there. The edicts of 1655 and 1686, which produced the Easter massacres and then the expulsion of the whole Waldensian population, went out from the administration seated in and around the town. The dictionary records Pinerolo because a persecuting power at the mouth of a valley is the ordinary condition of the church rather than an interruption of it, and Scripture says so without softening: “Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines persecution as the infliction of pain or death for adherence to a particular creed; a garrison as a body of troops stationed in a fort; and tribulation as severe affliction, distresses of life.
webster_full: PERSECUTION, n. The act or practice of persecuting; the infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed.
GARRISON, n. A body of troops stationed in a fort or fortified town; also, the fort or town itself.
TRIBULATION, n. [L. tribulatio.] Severe affliction; distresses of life; vexations.
CITADEL, n. [It. cittadella.] A fortress or castle in or near a city, intended for its defense, or to keep the inhabitants in subjection.
scriptures: Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.
Mat 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
corruption_summary: The Savoyard and French fortress at the mouth of the valleys, from which the edicts of 1655 and 1686 were administered.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the use of the civil sword to suppress a confession, which Rome urged and the dukes of Savoy and the king of France carried out. The 1655 massacres were an act of state against unarmed villages and were defended at the time as the enforcement of lawful religion. The dictionary names it as murder and notes that Protestant states committed the same sin where they had the chance; the error is not confessional but is the belief that faith can be commanded by force.

The principle to recover is that persecution is promised, that it is not a sign of God's displeasure, and that its term is fixed. Christ tells a church exactly what is coming and how long, bidding them “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10). Paul confirmed the young churches with the same unwelcome doctrine, “that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God” (Act 14:22). And the beatitude pronounces the verdict in advance: “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 5:10).

roots_lines: Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue, to persecute, to press after; 2 Timothy 3:12.
Greek thlipsis (G2347) — pressure, affliction, tribulation; Acts 14:22.

“be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10) — the Easter massacres of 1655.
“that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God” (Act 14:22) — the expulsion edict of 1686.

pos: n. (Alpine valley of the upper Chisone, Piedmont; a Waldensian valley on the French side whose people were exiled in 1686)
etymology: From Italian Pragelato, the frozen meadow; prato, meadow, and gelato, frozen.
biblical_def: Pragelato, the valley of the upper Chisone, was Waldensian like the others but lay on the French side of the watershed, and its people therefore came under the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685 a year before their brethren came under the Savoyard edict of 1686. They were given the choice of the mass or exile, and most took exile, walking out over the passes to Switzerland and from there to Wurttemberg, Hesse and Brandenburg, where their descendants kept French-speaking Waldensian congregations for generations. Three years later Henri Arnaud's nine hundred came back over the same ground. The dictionary records Pragelato because the deportation of a whole valley and the return of a part of it are the two halves of a promise Scripture makes to exiles. “And the ransomed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads” (Isa 35:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exile as banishment, the state of being expelled from one's country; a revocation as the act of recalling or annulling; and ransomed as redeemed, delivered by the payment of a price.
webster_full: EXILE, n. [L. exilium.] Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country; also, the person banished.
REVOCATION, n. [L. revocatio.] The act of recalling; a calling back; the state of being recalled; repeal; reversal.
RANSOM, v.t. [Fr. rancon.] To redeem from captivity or punishment by paying an equivalent; to buy off.
DEPORT, v.t. [L. deporto.] To transport; to carry away; to remove from one country to another by authority.
scriptures: And the ransomed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.
Ezr 1:5

Then rose up the chief of the fathers of Judah and Benjamin, and the priests, and the Levites, with all them whose spirit God had raised, to go up to build the house of the LORD which is in Jerusalem.
And gathered them out of the lands, from the east, and from the west, from the north, and from the south.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
corruption_summary: The upper Chisone valley, emptied by the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685; its exiles founded Waldensian colonies in Germany.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the revocation itself: a state withdrawing a sworn guarantee of liberty of conscience from its own subjects, and presenting their expulsion as a mercy that spared them worse. Louis XIV was congratulated across Catholic Europe for it. The dictionary names it as perjury compounded by cruelty, and notes that the Reformed states which received the refugees had in other places done similar things on a smaller scale.

The principle to recover is that God gathers His scattered people and that the believer's security was never in a charter or a valley. Ezra records the stirring of the exiles' own hearts for the return, naming “all them whose spirit God had raised, to go up to build the house of the LORD” (Ezr 1:5). The psalmist describes the gathering from every quarter, “from the east, and from the west, from the north, and from the south” (Psa 107:3). And Hebrews removes the whole question from the map: “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14).

“from the east, and from the west, from the north, and from the south” (Psa 107:3) — colonies in Wurttemberg, Hesse and Brandenburg.

pos: n. (town at the head of Lake Como, under the Grisons at the Reformation; a church of Italian evangelical refugees)
etymology: From Latin Clavenna, probably the key or the lock, from its command of the Alpine passes.
biblical_def: Chiavenna lay just inside the territory the Protestant Grisons held south of the Alps, which made it the first town of refuge for Italians fleeing the Roman Inquisition. An evangelical congregation gathered there from the 1540s under Agostino Mainardi, formerly an Augustinian provincial, and after him under Scipione Lentulo; Francesco Negri the humanist lived and wrote in the town. It was a quarrelsome church, because refugee churches are, and Mainardi spent years contending against the antitrinitarian and anabaptist opinions that Italian exiles were as liable to as to the Reformed faith. The dictionary records Chiavenna because the refugee congregation is a New Testament institution, and because Luke records that the first one was both a product of persecution and the origin of the Gentile mission. Those scattered by the death of Stephen “travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch” (Act 11:19), and at Antioch some of them began preaching to Greeks.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a refugee as one who flees to a place of safety, one who flees his country for safety; to scatter as to disperse, to separate and drive in different directions; and a sojourner as one who dwells in a place for a time.
webster_full: REFUGEE, n. [Fr. refugie.] One who flees to a place of safety; one who, in times of persecution or political commotion, flees to a foreign country for safety.
SCATTER, v.t. To disperse; to dissipate; to separate and drive in different directions.
SOJOURNER, n. One who dwells in a place for a time; a temporary resident; a stranger.
CONTEND, v.i. [L. contendo.] To strive; to struggle in opposition; to strive in debate; to dispute earnestly.
scriptures: Now they which were scattered abroad upon the persecution that arose about Stephen travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch, preaching the word to none but unto the Jews only.
And some of them were men of Cyprus and Cyrene, which, when they were come to Antioch, spake unto the Grecians, preaching the Lord Jesus.
Act 8:1

And Saul was consenting unto his death. And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria, except the apostles.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
corruption_summary: The first town of refuge south of the Alps for Italians fleeing the Inquisition; an evangelical congregation there from the 1540s.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the one that actually broke the Italian evangelical movement, and it came from inside: the antitrinitarianism that drew away men like Lelio Sozzini and Camillo Renato, who arrived among the exiles having rejected Rome and went on to reject the Trinity, the atonement and infant baptism in the same motion. Mainardi contended against it for years and is sometimes blamed for being contentious. He was right to contend. A church that will not discipline error among refugees will not remain a church.

The principle to recover is that God uses the scattering of His people as the means of spreading the gospel, and that the exile's citizenship is not in the town that received him. Luke records the dispersal plainly, that at the persecution after Stephen “they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria” (Act 8:1). From that scattering came the first preaching to Greeks, when men of Cyprus and Cyrene at Antioch “spake unto the Grecians, preaching the Lord Jesus” (Act 11:20). And the refugee is reminded where his city is: “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14).

pos: n. (Alpine valley of the upper Adda, held by the Grisons; scene of the Sacro Macello, the massacre of its Protestants in 1620)
etymology: From Italian Valtellina, the valley of Teglio, the chief place of the upper valley.
biblical_def: The Valtellina was a Catholic valley governed by the Protestant Grisons, and the arrangement held for eighty years and then broke. Reformed congregations were planted in the valley from the 1550s, mostly of Italian refugees and Grison settlers, and resentment at rule by heretics was worked on by Spanish and Austrian agents who wanted the valley as a military corridor between Milan and the Tyrol. On 19 July 1620 the rising came: between three and six hundred Protestants, including the pastors and the whole congregations of several villages, were killed over several days in what Italian history calls the Sacro Macello, the Holy Slaughter. The dictionary records it because the name the killers gave the act is itself the doctrine under judgment. John sees such souls and records what they say: “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a massacre as the murder of a number of human beings with cruelty and against the usages of nations; to avenge as to vindicate by inflicting punishment; and testimony as a solemn declaration made to establish a fact.
webster_full: MASSACRE, n. [Fr. massacre.] The murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers of human beings, with cruelty or atrocity, or contrary to the usages of nations.
AVENGE, v.t. To take satisfaction for an injury by punishing the injuring party; to vindicate by inflicting pain or evil on the wrongdoer.
TESTIMONY, n. [L. testimonium.] A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact.
ALTAR, n. [L. altare.] A mount; an elevation of earth, stone or other material, on which sacrifices were offered.
scriptures: Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
Rev 6:10
And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?
Rev 19:2
For true and righteous are his judgments: for he hath judged the great whore, which did corrupt the earth with her fornication, and hath avenged the blood of his servants at her hand.
Rom 8:36
As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.
corruption_summary: The Grison-ruled valley where three to six hundred Protestants were killed in July 1620, in the massacre its perpetrators called holy.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is named in the event's own title. To call a massacre holy is to assert that the killing of the baptised for their confession is an act of worship, and that assertion was made by men who had been taught it by a church which had authorised crusades against the Waldenses and an inquisition against the Italian evangelicals. The dictionary does not accept the plea of political provocation; Spanish and Austrian agents supplied the opportunity, but the theology that made murder a service to God was supplied by Rome.

The principle to recover is that the blood of the martyrs is heard, recorded and answered. The souls under the altar are given a voice and a question: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?” (Rev 6:10). The answer comes at the end of the book, when God “hath avenged the blood of his servants at her hand” (Rev 19:2). Paul meanwhile tells the church to expect nothing else: “For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter” (Rom 8:36). Abel's case established the rule at the beginning, for “the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground” (Gen 4:10).

pos: n. (region of north-west Italy, the duchy of Savoy; the Waldensian homeland and the scene of the massacres of 1655)
etymology: From Italian Piemonte, the foot of the mountains; pie, foot, and monte, mountain.
biblical_def: Piedmont was the duchy of Savoy and the home of the Waldensian church, and in April 1655 its government ordered the Protestants of the plain to withdraw into the high valleys in the depth of winter and then sent troops after them. The killing that followed, village by village over several weeks, became known across Europe as the Piedmontese Easter; Milton wrote the sonnet beginning with the appeal to avenge the slaughtered saints, Cromwell sent an embassy and raised money, and the Swiss and Dutch protested formally. A peace was patched up at Pinerolo the same year and broke down again in 1686. The dictionary records the region because the response of the wider church to the news is the part of the story that applies to every generation. Hebrews makes the duty an exercise of imagination rather than sentiment: “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines adversity as an event or series of events which oppose success or well-being, affliction; to remember as to have in mind, to bear in mind with esteem; and slaughter as the killing of men in battle, carnage.
webster_full: ADVERSITY, n. [L. adversitas.] An event or series of events which oppose success or desire; misfortune; calamity; affliction; distress.
REMEMBER, v.t. To have in the mind an idea which had been in the mind before; to bear in mind with esteem, or to regard.
SLAUGHTER, n. A killing; destruction of life by violence; carnage; butchery; great destruction of life.
BONDS, n. plural. Imprisonment; captivity; the state of being in chains or in prison.
scriptures: Heb 13:3
Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.

And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.
Mat 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
corruption_summary: The duchy of Savoy and Waldensian homeland; the Easter massacres of 1655 drew protest from Milton, Cromwell, the Swiss and the Dutch.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the one the dictionary has named throughout this seam, the state killing its subjects for their confession at the urging of a church that taught it to. What Piedmont adds is the test it set the rest of Protestant Europe, which had to decide whether a mountain people of no political or commercial value were worth the trouble of noticing. England, Switzerland and the Netherlands did notice, and the money and the diplomatic pressure saved lives. The matching failure is the modern one: a church that follows the sufferings of its own nation's believers and knows nothing of the rest.

The principle to recover is the solidarity of the whole body in the sufferings of any part, and the rest promised to those who do not survive. The psalmist puts the church's condition in the first person and does not explain it away: “Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter” (Psa 44:22). John is commanded to write the verdict on the martyrs, “Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth” (Rev 14:13), that they may rest from their labours. And the beatitude already names them heirs: “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10).

pos: n. (walled city of Tuscany; its Augustinian priory under Peter Martyr Vermigli became an evangelical centre until 1542)
etymology: From Latin Luca, probably from a Ligurian word for a marsh or a sacred grove.
biblical_def: Lucca came nearer to becoming a Protestant city than any other place in Italy. Peter Martyr Vermigli was prior of the Augustinian house of San Frediano from 1541, with the right of visitation over the city's clergy, and he used the position to lecture on the Psalms and on Paul's epistles, to appoint teachers of Greek and Hebrew, and to preach justification by faith to the merchant families of a republic that governed itself. When the Roman Inquisition was reconstituted in 1542 he fled to Zurich and then to Strasbourg, Oxford and Zurich again; a considerable number of Lucchese merchants followed him into exile in Geneva and Lyons, where their names appear in the registers for a century. The dictionary records Lucca because a promising work cut off at the root is not therefore a wasted one. “Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit” (Joh 12:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a prior as the superior of a convent of monks; stony as full of stones, hard; and to endure as to last, to continue in the same state without perishing.
webster_full: PRIOR, n. [L. prior.] The superior of a convent of monks, or one next in dignity to an abbot.
STONY, adj. Made of stone; full of stones; abounding with stones; hard, as a stony heart.
ENDURE, v.i. To last; to continue in the same state without perishing; to remain; to abide.
REPUBLIC, n. [L. respublica.] A commonwealth; a state in which the exercise of the sovereign power is lodged in representatives elected by the people.
scriptures: Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.
But he that received the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it;
Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended.
For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus unto Dalmatia.
corruption_summary: Vermigli was prior here from 1541 and preached justification to a self-governing republic; he fled in 1542 and Lucchese merchants followed him.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption that closed Lucca was the reconstitution of the Roman Inquisition in 1542, a deliberate decision to suppress the Italian evangelical movement by terror rather than to answer it, and it worked. Within twenty years the movement was destroyed, its leaders exiled or burnt, and Italy had no Protestant church outside the Alpine valleys. The dictionary names this as the corruption it is and adds the honest observation that many Italian evangelicals also failed the test when it came, conforming outwardly while believing otherwise, which is the error the Waldenses renounced at Chanforan.

The principle to recover is that a profession which cannot survive persecution was never rooted, and that the Lord said so in advance. The stony ground hearer “heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it” (Mat 13:20), and then fails on the one point that matters: “Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended” (Mat 13:21). Paul names one such man without ceremony, “For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world” (2Ti 4:10).

pos: n. (republic and city of the Adriatic; the printing capital of Catholic Europe and a early channel of evangelical books into Italy)
etymology: From Latin Venetia, the land of the Veneti; Italian Venezia.
biblical_def: Venice was the printing capital of southern Europe and therefore, for a generation, the chief channel by which evangelical doctrine entered Italy. Its presses turned out Bibles, Erasmus, and the anonymous Beneficio di Cristo of 1543, which sold perhaps forty thousand copies before it was suppressed and is the one Italian evangelical book that reached a mass readership. The republic guarded its independence against Rome jealously, resisted the papal interdict of 1606 under Paolo Sarpi, and refused for years to let the Inquisition work on its territory without Venetian magistrates present. It also, in the end, let the Inquisition work: heretics were drowned quietly in the lagoon, and the presses were censored. The dictionary records Venice because it is the clearest case of a state that would defy the pope over jurisdiction and not over the gospel. “they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God” (Joh 12:43).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an interdict as a prohibition, and in the Romish church a prohibition of the clergy from performing divine service; a press as a machine for printing; and to confess as to own, to acknowledge, to avow.
webster_full: INTERDICT, n. [L. interdictum.] A prohibition; in the Romish church, a prohibition of the pope, restraining the clergy from performing divine service.
PRESS, n. A machine for printing; also, the art or business of printing and publishing.
CONFESS, v.t. [L. confiteor.] To own, acknowledge or avow, as a crime, a fault, a charge, a debt, or something that is against one's interest or reputation.
LAGOON, n. [It. laguna.] A shallow lake or channel of water connected with the sea.
scriptures: Nevertheless among the chief rulers also many believed on him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they should be put out of the synagogue:
For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.
Mar 4:19
And the cares of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things entering in, choke the word, and it becometh unfruitful.
Mat 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
corruption_summary: The printing capital that carried evangelical books into Italy, and the republic that defied the pope over jurisdiction but not over doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the fear of men dressed as prudence of state. Venice had the presses, the independence, the lawyers and the nerve to resist an interdict, and it used all of them to protect its sovereignty and none of them to protect the gospel; when the choice came between trade with Catholic Europe and the toleration of evangelical preaching, it chose trade and drowned the preachers. The modern version needs no lagoon. It consists in a believing man's calculation that a particular truth is not worth what saying it would cost him.

The principle to recover is that the fear of man is a snare which Scripture describes with unusual precision. John reports rulers who genuinely believed and would not say so: “among the chief rulers also many believed on him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him” (Joh 12:42), and he gives the reason without charity. Christ names the agents that strangle a word already received, “the cares of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches” (Mar 4:19), which choke it so that it becomes unfruitful. And He blesses the opposite choice and its cost together (Mat 5:10).
